title: Oil at the threshold
hook: in the house where praise is sung, friends pour oil at the door for the bride, whose day has come (Gauri Deepaki M1, ang 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was jai ghar keerat: in the house where praise is sung. What did your home sound like in its last hour? Today, the same hymn, its last verses. Day four hundred twenty-three.
screen: `JAI GHAR KEERAT — IN THE HOUSE OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: A Punjabi wedding doesn't start on the wedding day. It starts weeks before, with a date. Someone fixes the auspicious day, it gets written down, and letters go out. Then the house fills up: cousins, aunties, songs every evening, turmeric, laughter, too much food. And at the doorway there is a small custom many families still keep. When the bride or the groom arrives at the threshold, a woman of the house pours a little oil on either side of the door, as a welcome and a blessing. Guru Nanak takes that whole scene and puts it at the end of his night song.
screen: `THE DATE IS FIXED AND WRITTEN.` → `SONGS EVERY EVENING.` → `OIL POURED AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The last verses of Sohila's first hymn sound like a wedding invitation. In paraphrase: the year and the moment have been written; come, friends, together, pour the oil. Give me your blessings, friends, so that I may meet my Lord. The word for that fixed date is saahaa, the wedding day set in advance. In Gurbani the soul is often pictured as a bride, and God as the beloved she longs to meet. So who is the bride here? The soul. And what is the wedding? The meeting with the One. Then the hymn turns, gently. In paraphrase again: into every house this message is sent; these calls come every day. Remember the One who sends the call, says Nanak; those days are drawing near. Many Sikhs hear the wedding here as death, the soul's day to go and meet the Beloved. That's why the verse belongs to a night song. Every night is a small rehearsal of letting go. But the mood is not dread. It's a wedding. The friends aren't weeping at the door; they're pouring oil and giving blessings. Notice, too, that the summons isn't sent to one unlucky house. It goes to every house, every day. Nobody is singled out. Nobody is skipped. The hymn doesn't ask you to fear the letter. It asks you to be the kind of house where praise is sung when it arrives, and to have friends at the door when it's your turn.
screen: `THE DATE IS WRITTEN: SAAHAA.` · `THE SOUL AS THE BRIDE.` · `A CALL TO EVERY HOUSE, EVERY DAY.` · `FRIENDS AT THE DOOR WITH BLESSINGS.` · then, large: `THE BRIDE IS CALLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless someone's doorway. Picture a door you know well: a parent's front door, a friend's apartment, a neighbor's gate, your own. See it clearly, the handle, the step, the light. Now imagine standing there as one of the friends in the hymn, wishing whoever lives inside well. Not a speech. Just: may this house be well. Hold that wish while you breathe. Then move to one more door if you like. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly for the people behind it. The bell holds the time.
Oil at the threshold. The wedding welcome Guru Nanak places at the end of Sohila's first hymn: friends bless the bride, the soul, whose day has been written.

Your line: the bride is called. Today, when you walk through a door, your own or anyone's, let it remind you that the call comes to every house, and wish the house well. Day four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite these verses every night as the close of Kirtan Sohila's first hymn, and the same hymn is sung at funerals; many Punjabi families still keep the custom of pouring oil at the threshold when a bride or groom arrives.

match.prompt: the wedding in the hymn — tap the pairs.
pairs: the wedding date, fixed in advance

myth: in the hymn, the summons goes to one unlucky house
it goes into every house, and the calls come every day.
Gurbani often pictures the soul as a bride
and God as the beloved she longs to meet.
the friends at the door are weeping
they pour oil and give blessings, as at a wedding.

fork.setup: the wedding date has been written, and the bride's day is near. what do her friends do?
options: shut the door and hope the day passes.
pour oil at the threshold and give their blessings.
argue about whether the date is right.
fork.reveal: the hymn asks the friends to come together, pour the oil and bless her, so she may meet her Lord.

original.note: Gurmukhi: saahaa, the fixed wedding date; in the hymn, the day the soul is called.

trapdoor: what you thought: the oil at the threshold is just a wedding detail.
what it means: the soul is the bride, her wedding is the meeting with God, and friends bless her as her day comes.
what a scholar hears: the verse borrows the Punjabi wedding custom of the fixed saahaa and oil at the doorway, and many commentators read the wedding as death.

sources.ref: Gauri Deepaki M1, Ang 12 (Kirtan Sohila, hymn 1, closing verses)

notes: Closing verses paraphrased ('the year and the moment have been written; come, friends, pour the oil; give me your blessings so that I may meet my Lord'; 'into every house this message is sent; these calls come every day'); confirm.
Wedding custom: oil poured on either side of the doorway when the bride or groom arrives (often called tel chona); confirm description and who performs it.
Reading the wedding as death: common in Sikh commentary and the reason the hymn is sung at funerals; confirm 'many Sikhs hear'.
Gurmukhi ਸਾਹਾ (the hymn's form may be inflected); confirm.
